name: Lithium carbonate
route_note: Oral tablets, capsules or liquid; dosed to a target serum level with regular monitoring.

discovery.note: Cade observed calming effects of lithium urate in guinea pigs and then treated ten manic patients, publishing in the Medical Journal of Australia.

tagline: Simple ion that remains the gold standard for bipolar disorder and suicide prevention
summary: Lithium salts are the oldest and best-established mood stabilisers, used for acute mania and long-term prevention of episodes in bipolar disorder. Lithium reduces suicide risk, but its narrow therapeutic index requires regular blood-level, kidney and thyroid monitoring.
mechanism: The exact mechanism is unknown. Lithium inhibits inositol monophosphatase and inositol polyphosphate 1-phosphatase, depleting inositol and dampening phosphoinositide signalling in overactive neurons (the inositol depletion hypothesis).

It also directly and indirectly inhibits glycogen synthase kinase-3β, influencing circadian rhythm, neuroplasticity and neuroprotection, and modulates glutamatergic, dopaminergic and serotonergic transmission.

history.title: Early use
history.detail: William Hammond uses lithium bromide for mania; lithium also features in 19th-century 'uric acid diathesis' treatments.

history.title: Cade's report
history.detail: John Cade reports lithium's effect in mania in the Medical Journal of Australia.

history.title: US salt substitute deaths
history.detail: Deaths from lithium chloride sold as a salt substitute lead to its US withdrawal.

history.title: Schou's trial
history.detail: Mogens Schou in Denmark conducts one of the first placebo-controlled trials in psychiatry with lithium.

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: The FDA approves lithium for mania; maintenance use follows in 1974.

history.title: Suicide meta-analysis
history.detail: A BMJ meta-analysis confirms lithium reduces suicide in mood disorders.

pk.half_life: About 18–36 hours (longer in elderly and renal impairment)
pk.excretion: Renal (~95%), reabsorbed with sodium in the proximal tubule

safety.boxed_warning: Lithium toxicity is closely related to serum concentrations and can occur at doses close to therapeutic levels; serum monitoring is required.

facts: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazide diuretics raise lithium levels.
Lithium is one of the few psychiatric drugs with consistent evidence of reducing suicide.
